title: Solid-state hydrogen storage materials
bottleneck: Storing hydrogen as a solid in metal hydrides or complex hydrides avoids extreme pressures, but no material yet meets all targets at once: high gravimetric capacity, fast kinetics near ambient temperature, and thousands of reversible cycles. Magnesium hydride holds plenty of hydrogen but releases it only above 300 C; lighter complex hydrides suffer from poor reversibility and toxic byproducts. The thermodynamics-kinetics trade-off has resisted decades of alloying.
why_it_blocks: Hydrogen vehicles and seasonal energy storage need compact, safe, low-pressure storage to be practical. Without it, storage means 700-bar carbon-fiber tanks — expensive, bulky, and energy-hungry to fill — which caps hydrogen's competitiveness against batteries.
current_state: Destabilized hydride mixtures and nanoconfined systems have lowered desorption temperatures in the lab, but cycle life and system-level capacity still fall short of DOE targets. Compressed gas remains the only deployed option.
